newsitem.title: USA: U.S. retailers' earnings exceed expectations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. retailers' earnings exceed expectations.

text.p: Four big retailers -- J.C. Penney Co. Inc., Dillard Department Stores Inc., TJX Cos. Inc. and Lands' End Inc. -- posted first-quarter earnings Tuesday that beat expectations on Wall Street, aided by fewer markdowns and strong sales.
J.C. Penney's earnings fell about 2 percent to $139 million, or 53 cents a share, from $142 million, or 57 cents a share, in the first quarter of last year.

Still, the results beat Wall Street analysts' forecast of 50 cents a share, according to First Call, which tracks earnings estimates. Penney's sales jumped 44 percent to $6.7 billion from $4.6 billion a year ago.

Plano, Texas-based Penney's earnings were hurt by weak performance at its core department stores and costs of swallowing drug store giant Eckerd Corp., which Penney acquired during the quarter in a deal valued at $3.3 billion.
Analysts had worried steep merchandise discounts at Penney's department stores took a big bite out of profits, but the damage from markdowns was not as bad as expected.
"We knew it was going to be a bad quarter," said Jeffrey Edelman of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Inc. "It wasn't quite as bad as we would have thought."
The company said operating profits at its Eckerd division rose 30 percent in the quarter. The integration of Eckerd has met expectations so far, it added.
Little Rock, Ark.-based Dillard said earnings rose 3 percent to $58.3 million, or 52 cents a share, from $56.4 million, or 50 cents a share, in the 1996 quarter.
Sales rose to $1.52 billion from $1.45 billion. Analysts had forecast earnings would be flat in the quarter, according to First Call.

TJX, based in Framingham, Mass., said net income jumped 61 percent to $48.5 million, or 54 cents a share, from $30.1 million, or 33 cents a share, in last year's first quarter. Sales rose to $1.56 billion from $1.47 billion.
The earnings were above Wall Street's consensus estimate of 51 cents a share.

The discount retailer said combined profits at its off-price apparel chains T.J. Maxx and Marshalls stores climbed by 62 percent during the first quarter. TJX acquired Marshalls from Melville Corp. for $606 million in 1995.

"The combined buying power of these two divisions, as well as expense savings resulting from the consolidation of Marshalls, were the two major drivers of the substantial year-over-year gains in this first quarter," said TJX President Bernard Cammarata.

Lands' End, the catalog retailer based in Dodgeville, Wis., said net income rose to $11.3 million, or 35 cents a share, in the quarter, including a $4.7 million gain from the sale of The Territory Ahead, a catalog company.

Minus the gain, earnings rose by 50 percent to $6.6 million, or 20 cents per share, from $4.4 million, or 13 cents a share, in the first quarter of 1996. Analysts had forecast earnings of 17 cents a share.
Sales rose 15 percent to $245 million.
Like other retailers, Lands' End did not load up on too much inventory this year and was able to avoid the clearance sales that eroded profits at many chains last year.
"A year ago, (retailers) probably came into Christmas with too much inventory and had to take markdowns in the first quarter," said Kevin Silverman of Everen Securities.
But this year, Lands' End and other companies kept inventories under better control.
"They're trying to be careful on inventory," Silverman said. "They've cut back on the things that didn't sell well."
J.C. Penney ended the quarter with a backlog of merchandise, and analysts worry that clearance sales could hurt profits in the second quarter.
"It implies that if sales don't really pick up in the May, earnings could be at risk as a result of markdowns in June and July," said Patrick McCormack of Alex. Brown & Sons Inc.
